L01.note: Only unpunctuated finite clause; A is a participle fragment, C/D put commas between subject and verb.

L02.note: Lean to the classic proximity trap (singular head noun before 'with eggs'), but the head noun itself varies so the sentence decides.

L03.note: 'but also' completes 'not only', and the nearer subject 'pattern books' takes plural 'offer'.

L05.note: Dangling-modifier set: the only option whose subject is the animate agent (the ornithologist); also the odd short one.

L06.note: Unpunctuated and 'casts' agrees with 'it'; the commas split a relative clause from its verb.

L07.note: Finite singular looks like a main verb; number of the withheld subject unknown.

L08.note: Modifier-placement set: the concise active clause with the owners as subject; B is illogical, C/D wordy or passive.

L09.note: 'but also to open it' keeps the infinitive parallel to a presumed 'not only to ...'.

L10.note: Subject-position compound needs nominative 'I'; the report/mine variants are distractor noise.

L11.note: One comma closing the introductory 'as X did' clause; A adds a subject-verb comma, C makes a fragment, D has none.

L13.note: Both pronouns are objects ('him', 'over whom'); the only option with consistent object case.

L15.note: 'most of whom' is the well-formed object form if the antecedent is people; 'most of which' equally possible for things.

L16.note: Absolute phrase closed by a comma; C is a comma splice, B lacks the comma, D isolates the participle.

L17.note: Classic 'to whoever' trap: the pronoun is subject of the following clause, and the preposition must be present.

L18.note: Reads like 'one of the longest rivers of Europe, is' with a singular head; weak.

L19.note: Three dash variants against one comma; taking the odd one out but the opening mark is withheld.

L21.note: 'not that ... but that' correlative; C/D break parallel with 'because'. Number of 'was' is a guess.

L22.note: Closing dash of an appositive pair plus plural verb for a two-item list; B is singular.

L23.note: Unpunctuated finite verb; the comma variants separate subject and verb.

L24.note: Balanced comma pair around the appositive; the dash/semicolon options mismatch the opening comma.

L25.note: Parallelism item with the list withheld; gerund is the likeliest partner.

L26.note: Plural for a 'together' compound; tense unknown.

L27.note: Unpunctuated, plural 'relays ... trip'; A adds a subject-verb comma, B/D mismatch number.

L28.note: Unpunctuated singular; number of the head noun is withheld.

L29.note: Object case after a preposition inside a closed parenthetical, so 'me,'; 'myself' is the reflexive distractor.

L31.note: Colon introducing an explanation reads like a key; C is a semicolon before a fragment.

L32.note: 'together with' does not pluralize the subject, and the commas are balanced; A/D mix number and punctuation.

L33.note: Semicolon-separated list with internal commas: item opens and closes with semicolons, appositive with a comma.

L34.note: 'whoever' as subject of its own clause; A adds a redundant 'that', C/D use object case.

L35.note: Comma after the introductory 'In October', then no mark between subject and verb.

L36.note: Restrictive 'that' with no comma; D 'lime, that' is a known distractor shape.

L37.note: 'whoever' is subject of 'had'; the 'having' variants are fragments.

L39.note: Dangling-modifier set: the only option with Dr. Halloran as grammatical subject.

L40.note: Restrictive 'those that formed'; A/C are set off unnecessarily, B is a spliced clause.

L41.note: The engineer, not the design, is 'backed by crews'; singular 'was' matches.

L42.note: Unpunctuated plural after 'bones'; head noun may differ.

L43.note: Unpunctuated singular with 'council' as a collective; weak.

L44.note: Balanced comma pair around the appositive; D mismatches comma with dash.
